Base directory for this skill: /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/.claude/skills/zimmerMANNReview

Review of a colleague's work. Same architecture as the build chain — ground truth, a gated audit,
then present and stop — tailored to a PR you did not write.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.**

**The thing that makes it work:** you hold the ground truth and the adjudication, and delegate only
the reading. Reviewers are cheap and fallible; measurements are expensive and authoritative. Keep
those on opposite sides of the line.

**Input:** `PR #79` — a PR number.

**Scale to the work.** A two-file PR does not get four reviewers. Nothing too crazy, no
overthinking.

---

## Phase 1 — ground truth. Yours, not an agent's.

### Frame the PR

Base SHA, head SHA, files changed, ±lines. **Use the live head** — a stale ref has already caused a
whole round of re-verification here.

### Requirements — Jira, Confluence, Figma

Build the same requirements picture a PreBuild would build, then judge the PR against it. Every
scope argument, every "this is missing", every "this wasn't asked for" gets decided against these
words — not the PR description's paraphrase of them.

**Jira.** Pull the full ticket: description, ACs, linked work items, and — critically — the full
comment thread. Decisions made in comments routinely contradict the description and never make it
back into the ACs. Flag: untestable ACs · requirements that contradict each other or the comments
· a linked blocker still open · a decision in comments that the implementation may not have seen ·
**evidence that a different PR, branch, or assignee is already working the same ticket.**

**Anything flagged here goes in your next status update to Marcel, even when it's correctly out
of scope for the PR itself.** "Not my concern for this review" and "not worth telling him" are
different judgements — a discovery can be exactly right to leave alone in the diff and still be
something he needs to know exists. Deciding not to act on it is not the same as deciding not to
mention it.

**Confluence.** If the ticket links a PRD, TSD, or integration doc, read it. The Jira ACs are
often a summary; the full requirements live in Confluence. Flag: a Confluence requirement not
reflected in the ACs · a doc that contradicts the ticket · a doc that describes an approach the
PR does not follow.

**Figma.** Read the design systematically — not just the node cited in the PR description.

- **All variants and states:** hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty, selected.
  A state the PR doesn't implement is a finding; a state Figma doesn't specify is an open
  question to name, not a reason to skip. **Before concluding a state is simply absent from a
  component, check whether an adjacent or parent element carries that same signal instead** (the
  button not the swatch, the row not the cell) — a concern can be fully handled by the design and
  still look like a gap if you only look at the one element it doesn't live on.
- **Annotations:** interaction notes and spacing/token callouts often hold the real spec detail.
- **Currency:** is the linked node archived or superseded? An archived node that still renders
  is a trap — triage before judging.
- **Tokenisation:** does every colour, spacing, and type value map to an existing `--zimm-*`
  token, or did the author introduce a new one? A new token is Tier 1; confirm it was handled
  correctly.
- **Measurement:** FRAMES and INSTANCES report real boxes (comparable to CSS). TEXT nodes report
  cap-height (not comparable). Never file a mismatch from a TEXT node. Never cross-compare the
  Design System file and the Designs file — they are different sources.

**If the Jira-linked nodes are incomplete, partial, or outdated — stop and ask Marcel for the
correct nodes before continuing.** One node URL per variant and per state, not one per component.
Do not guess at a neighbouring node that looks close, do not proceed on a partial picture, and do
not treat an archived node as the spec. The whole review hangs on having the right design source;
a wrong node produces false findings and misses real ones. This is the one step where asking
beats estimating.

The visual checklist in Phase 2 tells you what to verify in the browser. This step tells you
**what to look for** — you cannot run that checklist without knowing what the design intended.

### The rubric

`.claude/rules/*`, `AGENTS.md`, and the exemplar PR the work should follow. These are what the PR
is judged against — a reviewer applying general best practice instead of house rules generates
noise that reads like signal.

**If the PR edits the rule files it would be judged against, read the rubric at the BASE commit.**
Judging a PR against its own edited rules is circular. Rule-file edits are reviewed separately, as
changes.

### Run the gates yourself — on head and on base

```
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run test
npm run lint
node scripts/auditTokenUsage.mjs
```

Then run them again at the base SHA. **Without a baseline you cannot tell a failure the PR
introduced from one it inherited**, and inherited debt reported as a new violation is the fastest
way to lose a reviewer's trust.

Three false signals, all seen on this repo:

1. **Non-zero at a healthy baseline.** `lint` and `audit:tokens` both exit non-zero on a clean
   tree. Compare counts; ignore exit codes.
2. **A pass having run nothing.** `vitest.config.ts` sets `passWithNoTests: true` — a typo'd path
   filter exits 0 having run zero tests. **Assert on the reported item count, never the exit code.**
3. **A skipped required check looks green.** `detect-changes` can skip `unit-tests` and
   `storybook-test` entirely, and the PR still shows mergeable. Report which checks actually
   *executed* versus which were skipped. A skip proves nothing.

### CodeRabbit is an input, not a verdict

If CodeRabbit has reviewed, read it — then verify it. It has run as low as 1-in-6 correct on this
repo. Its findings enter Phase 2 as claims to test, exactly like anyone else's.

---

## Phase 2 — audit

### Fan out

`zm-tester` dispatches reviewers on **distinct but overlapping** briefs. The overlap is the
mechanism: two agents converging independently is your confidence signal; two disagreeing is where
you learn something.

Give each: the diff, the ticket verbatim, and **your measured gate numbers — then forbid them from
re-running the gates.** Their budget goes on what the gates cannot see.

Angles that have earned their place: correctness and regression · conventions, structure and tier
ownership · contract fidelity, if the PR ports, wraps or overrides something · failure modes and
security · token and styling strategy (bandaid tokens, missing semantic tokens, state
exhaustiveness).

**Design fidelity is yours, not an agent's.** Agents have no browser and no Figma access — ask
them to reason from code and they will, but they cannot see what renders. For any PR that changes
rendered output, run this checklist yourself at the PR's head:

| What to check | How |
|---|---|
| Dimensions and spacing match Figma frames | DevTools computed, vs. Figma inspect |
| Colours resolve to the correct semantic token | DevTools → Computed → colour value |
| Typography uses `textStyle=`, not raw `fontSize` | DevTools → font-size is a `var()` |
| All designed states render correctly (hover, focus, active, disabled) | Tab through + `:hov` in DevTools |
| Responsive behaviour matches the spec | Resize or toggle responsive mode |
| No visual regressions on adjacent components | Scroll the surrounding page |

If a state is not in the PR's recipe at all, no agent will flag it — only you will notice. The
visual checkpoint is the only gate on design fidelity.

Use **fresh contexts, not forks.** A fork inherits your assumptions about what "done" looks like,
which is exactly what you want tested.

### Scope

`zm-orchestrator` returns the scope verdict — does this PR deliver its ticket, neither under nor
over. Both directions carry equal weight.

### Verify the findings before they reach you

`zm-scorer`, briefed in **findings mode** — it is not scoring the PR, it is scoring the claims:

> For each finding: does it survive scrutiny? Reproduce it or say you could not. Return
> **CONFIRMED** (reproduced from source), **PLAUSIBLE** (consistent with what you read, decisive
> evidence missing — say exactly what would settle it), or **UNSUPPORTED** (the citation does not
> support the claim; say what is actually true). Where a finding's conclusion is broader than its
> search supports, downgrade it — that is the single most common failure mode. Any "X exists
> nowhere" claim must state its search scope in the same sentence.

Expect roughly a third to be wrong. You should not be adjudicating unverified claims.

**This applies to your own findings too, not just an agent's.** Anything you notice directly
while gathering ground truth (a comparison against a related PR, a claim sitting in a code
comment, an assumption about what a value implies) gets the same CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE/UNSUPPORTED
discipline before it is presented as fact — a finding is not exempt from scrutiny just because no
agent produced it. Route it through the same questions: what is the search scope, does one
uncorroborated source actually settle this, and has a stated number been measured or only assumed.

### Classify every survivor

- **In-scope defect** — belongs to this PR. Only these can become comments.
- **Out-of-scope** — real, but not this PR's problem. Name the owning ticket or the person.
- **Nitpick** — cosmetic, brings no value. Recorded, never posted.

A true finding raised on the wrong PR is still noise.

---

## Phase 3 — adjudicate

### Present, in "ELI5 but I'm the FED Lead" register

1. **Gate table** — head versus base, with which checks actually executed
2. **Findings, ranked by what it costs to ignore** — not by severity label, by consequence.
   Each with `file:line`, CONFIRMED or PLAUSIBLE, and its classification
3. **The scope verdict**
4. **What nobody verified** — the honest section, and what stops a clean result reading as proof
5. **Your adjudications to make**, one at a time via AskUserQuestion

### The verdict is yours

**Approve or request changes is your call, and so is every disputed finding.** The agents produce
findings; you decide what they mean. Where two reviewers disagree, go to source yourself — do not
average them, and do not take the more confident one. Confidence and correctness are not correlated
in agent output.

Name one premise every reviewer agreed on, and make someone attack it.

### Then the comments

Draft general and inline comments for the in-scope defects only. Structure that has worked:

- Verdict up front
- The small cleanups separated from the one thing that genuinely needs the author's call
- A blocker framed as **a question about intent**, citing the project's own doc by section
- The two acceptable resolutions named
- Where an independent tool corroborated, say so

**Natural human language without sacrificing the technical accuracy.** No em-dashes. No Claude or
CodeRabbit attribution. No citation of any local-only doc — cite `AGENTS.md` or `.claude/rules/*`
instead, which the author can actually open. No opening praise or thanks before the substance — a
review comment states findings, it does not warm up first. Watch for jargon-stacking too: a
sentence naming three technical concepts back to back reads like documentation, not like one
person explaining something to another — split it or say it plainer instead.

**Never reveal that a parallel or competing implementation of the same ticket exists**, even in
passing ("the other version of this feature," "the other build") — a review comment is visible to
the whole team, and disclosing a second, independent attempt at the same story is not this
reviewer's call to make. When a content rule like this applies, sweep every drafted comment for
it before presenting the batch, not just the one currently under discussion — a rule caught on
one comment and missed on a near-identical one is a leak, not a style nit.

**Nothing posts until you say so.** Show the full set, post the batch on your go.

---

## The loop

The author pushes changes. Re-review.

**Scoped by default:** which findings the new commits resolved, which they missed, and whether the
fixes introduced anything new. Settled items are not re-litigated.

**Full pass when the diff has genuinely moved** — a substantial new commit, or a change to the
approach rather than the details. **Say which one you ran.**

Repeat until approved. Confirm your own requested changes actually landed rather than taking
"done" on trust.

---

## Ownership and phrasing — every outward-facing surface

Every finding names **who resolves it**: the author, Tim, a designer, a BA, QA.

**Where the owner is senior or lateral, phrase it as a question — never a directive.** "Should this
route via X, or have I misread it?" not "change this to X." Ask confirmatorily.

Before posting, count the asks. A review that mentions one person eight times reads as hiding
behind their authority.

**Be scrupulously fair to the author.** Separate "broke a documented rule" from "hit a gap the
process never covered", and where the process failed them, say so. Flag explicitly any finding
where the fact is true but the characterisation is unfair — better to drop a finding than post an
unfair one.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never write code.** This skill reviews. If a fix is needed on your own branch, that is Build.
- **Never post a comment, a review, or a verdict without an explicit go.**
- **Never resolve a thread you did not open.**
- **Never report inherited debt as a new violation.** Baseline first.
- **Never flag out-of-scope findings onto the PR.** Record them for yourself.
- **Say what you could not verify.** A review that finds nothing has not been shown to be capable
  of finding anything.

addedLines: - agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-py: Use this agent to verify that a Python Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a Python Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)

- agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-ts: Use this agent to verify that a TypeScript Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a TypeScript Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- plugin-dev:agent-creator: Use this agent when the user asks to "create an agent", "generate an agent", "build a new agent", "make me an agent that...", or describes agent functionality they need. Trigger when user wants to create autonomous agents for plugins. Examples:

<example>
Context: User wants to create a code review agent
user: "Create an agent that reviews code for quality issues"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate the agent configuration."
<commentary>
User requesting new agent creation, trigger agent-creator to generate it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User describes needed functionality
user: "I need an agent that generates unit tests for my code"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to create a test generation agent."
<commentary>
User describes agent need, trigger agent-creator to build it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants to add agent to plugin
user: "Add an agent to my plugin that validates configurations"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate a configuration validator agent."
<commentary>
Plugin development with agent addition, trigger agent-creator.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Write, Read)

- plugin-dev:plugin-validator: Use this agent when the user asks to "validate my plugin", "check plugin structure", "verify plugin is correct", "validate plugin.json", "check plugin files", or mentions plugin validation. Also trigger proactively after user creates or modifies plugin components. Examples:

<example>
Context: User finished creating a new plugin
user: "I've created my first plugin with commands and hooks"
assistant: "Great! Let me validate the plugin structure."
<commentary>
Plugin created, proactively validate to catch issues early.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the plugin."
</example>

<example>
Context: User explicitly requests validation
user: "Validate my plugin before I publish it"
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to perform comprehensive validation."
<commentary>
Explicit validation request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified plugin.json
user: "I've updated the plugin manifest"
assistant: "Let me validate the changes."
<commentary>
Manifest modified, validate to ensure correctness.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the manifest."
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- plugin-dev:skill-reviewer: Use this agent when the user has created or modified a skill and needs quality review, asks to "review my skill", "check skill quality", "improve skill description", or wants to ensure skill follows best practices. Trigger proactively after skill creation. Examples:

<example>
Context: User just created a new skill
user: "I've created a PDF processing skill"
assistant: "Great! Let me review the skill quality."
<commentary>
Skill created, proactively trigger skill-reviewer to ensure it follows best practices.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the skill."
</example>

<example>
Context: User requests skill review
user: "Review my skill and tell me how to improve it"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to analyze the skill quality."
<commentary>
Explicit skill review request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified skill description
user: "I updated the skill description, does it look good?"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the changes."
<commentary>
Skill description modified, review for triggering effectiveness.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

- zm-implementer: Executes one step of a Zimmermann PWA Kit build plan. Use when a planned step needs to be implemented in code. Writes only the files the step names, and stops rather than expanding scope. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-orchestrator: Scope and spec-conformance checker for an in-flight Zimmermann build. Use after an implementation step to judge whether the work delivers exactly what the plan specified — neither less nor more. Reports a verdict; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-planner: Synthesises gathered evidence into an executable build plan for a Zimmermann PWA Kit story. Use after all sources have been gathered, when the findings need to become a sequenced plan with per-step pass criteria. Does not gather evidence itself and does not write code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, WebFetch)

- zm-scorer: Scores an implemented and tested Zimmermann build step and decides PASS or return-to-implementer. Use after the Tester reports. Judges quality against six axes; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-tester: Tests an implemented Zimmermann build step across multiple angles and reports findings. Use after the Implementer reports a step done. Finds and reports problems; never fixes them. Dispatches its own sub-agents for parallel angles. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

## ac642cf1-e1c8-4490-9caa-814476453870
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

{"additions":132,"author":{"id":"MDQ6VXNlcjI5NDcyOTg2","is_bot":false,"login":"TimLavelleACC","name":""},"baseRefName":"develop","baseRefOid":"a4f6921330a280a79cdf54343a1edc5c3c508318","body":"## Summary

Supersedes #76, which was built against a stale worktree branch (359 commits
behind `origin/develop`) that was missing `overrides/app/theme/fontFace.tsx`
and `overrides/app/theme/zimmTokensGlobal.tsx` entirely. This PR re-verifies
the same design against the real, current codebase and adjusts it for two
components #76 never accounted for. #76 will be closed in favour of this PR.

- Closes the Lighthouse `csp-xss` finding for `style-src` by replacing the
  paired `'self' 'unsafe-inline'` (Chakra UI's runtime style injection
  requirement, per the pre-existing comment in `contentSecurityPolicy.ts`)
  with a per-request nonce. `'unsafe-inline'` is kept alongside it only as
  the standard CSP3 legacy-browser fallback — per spec, any browser that
  understands `'nonce-...'` ignores `'unsafe-inline'` in the same directive,
  so this doesn't reopen what the nonce closes for real users.
- **No `overrides/app/ssr.js` change required.** helmet 4.6.0's CSP
  directive values accept a `(req, res) => string` function, invoked per
  request, so the nonce is generated and cached on `res.locals.cspNonce`
  entirely from `overrides/app/ssr/contentSecurityPolicy.ts`. `ssr.js`
  already passes this config through to `helmet()` as a plain value,
  re-evaluated every request — confirmed against
  `helmet/dist/middlewares/content-security-policy/index.d.ts` and
  `@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk`'s `react-rendering.js` (which passes
  `res.locals` straight through as `AppConfig`'s `locals` prop).
- `_app-config` wraps `ChakraProvider` **and everything rendered inside it**
  — `ZimmFontFace` and `ZimmTokensGlobal`'s raw `@emotion/react` `<Global>`
  elements, plus `UiCopyProvider`/`children` — in an `@emotion/react`
  `CacheProvider` configured with that nonce
  (`createCache({key: 'css', nonce})`, the officially documented emotion CSP
  mechanism). `<Global>` reads the same ambient emotion cache context Chakra
  itself does, so wrapping `CacheProvider` around `ChakraProvider` (rather
  than only around Chakra's own internals) covers all three:
  - **Server-side:** nonce arrives via `res.locals` → the `locals` prop.
  - **Client-side:** `ssr/browser/main.jsx` hydrates with a fresh,
    request-context-free `locals` object, so the nonce is instead read back
    off a `<meta name="csp-nonce">` tag emitted server-side via the existing
    `react-helmet` pipeline (`Helmet.renderStatic()` already collects into
    `<head>`; `react-helmet`'s ambient module declaration already exists in
    `overrides/app/types/vendor.d.ts` — no new type declaration needed here).

## Out of scope / not fixable from this repo

- `script-src`'s `'unsafe-eval'` is added by the MRT platform layer, not by
  this repo's own CSP config. Not fixable from any file in this repo.
- `script-src`'s third-party host allowlist (Stripe/PayPal/Adyen/Google
  Pay/Maps/Measmerize) is a legitimate requirement for those vendors'
  externally-hosted SDK scripts — nonce-based CSP doesn't replace host
  allowlisting for external `<script src>` origins, only inline scripts.

## Governance note

This change touches both a **Tier 1** file
(`overrides/app/ssr/contentSecurityPolicy.ts`) and a **Tier 2** file
(`overrides/app/components/_app-config/index.tsx`) in one PR. Per
`AGENTS.md` Hard Rule 10 this would normally require stopping to confirm
scope first, but the coupling is inherent to the fix itself — the nonce has
to reach both the helmet config and every emotion consumer nested inside
`ChakraProvider` — and was the explicit investigation scope of the SFCC-856
task. Tier 1 edit made under the verified-session exception in AGENTS.md's
Tier 1 Approval section — authenticated `gh` identity `TimLavelleACC`
confirmed as a member of `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` before editing
`contentSecurityPolicy.ts`.

- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` — passes
- [x] `npx eslint` on both changed files — passes

      deploying. Needs a real SIT/preview deployment + Lighthouse check

      half, specifically — see "Out of scope" above for `script-src`).
- [ ] Suggest a manual smoke check on that deployment: confirm Chakra
      styling, the self-hosted Futura Round font, and the `--zimm-*` custom
      properties all render correctly, and the browser devtools console
      shows no CSP violations for `style-src`.

  requirement, per the pre-existing comment in `contentSecurityPolicy.ts`)
  with a per-request nonce. `'unsafe-inline'` is kept alongside it only as
  the standard CSP3 legacy-browser fallback — per spec, any browser that
  understands `'nonce-...'` ignores `'unsafe-inline'` in the same directive,
  so this doesn't reopen what the nonce closes for real users.
- **No `overrides/app/ssr.js` change required.** helmet 4.6.0's CSP
  directive values accept a `(req, res) => string` function, invoked per
  request, so the nonce is generated and cached on `res.locals.cspNonce`
  entirely from `overrides/app/ssr/contentSecurityPolicy.ts`. `ssr.js`
  already passes this config through to `helmet()` as a plain value,
  re-evaluated every request — confirmed against
  `helmet/dist/middlewares/content-security-policy/index.d.ts` and
  `@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk`'s `react-rendering.js` (which passes
  `res.locals` straight through as `AppConfig`'s `locals` prop).
- `_app-config` wraps `ChakraProvider` **and everything rendered inside it**
  — `ZimmFontFace` and `ZimmTokensGlobal`'s raw `@emotion/react` `<Global>`
  elements, plus `UiCopyProvider`/`children` — in an `@emotion/react`
  `CacheProvider` configured with that nonce
  (`createCache({key: 'css', nonce})`, the officially documented emotion CSP
  mechanism). `<Global>` reads the same ambient emotion cache context Chakra
  itself does, so wrapping `CacheProvider` around `ChakraProvider` (rather
  than only around Chakra's own internals) covers all three:
  - **Server-side:** nonce arrives via `res.locals` → the `locals` prop.
  - **Client-side:** `ssr/browser/main.jsx` hydrates with a fresh,
    request-context-free `locals` object, so the nonce is instead read back
    off a `<meta name="csp-nonce">` tag emitted server-side via the existing
    `react-helmet` pipeline (`Helmet.renderStatic()` already collects into
    `<head>`; `react-helmet`'s ambient module declaration already exists in
    `overrides/app/types/vendor.d.ts` — no new type declaration needed here).

## Out of scope / not fixable from this repo

- `script-src`'s `'unsafe-eval'` is added by the MRT platform layer, not by
  this repo's own CSP config. Not fixable from any file in this repo.
- `script-src`'s third-party host allowlist (Stripe/PayPal/Adyen/Google
  Pay/Maps/Measmerize) is a legitimate requirement for those vendors'
  externally-hosted SDK scripts — nonce-based CSP doesn't replace host
  allowlisting for external `<script src>` origins, only inline scripts.

name: Protected File Guard

# Server-side enforcement of the tier/squad model. The client-side
# .claude/hooks/tier2Warn.sh is non-blocking — this workflow is the
# authoritative gate at PR time.

on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - develop
      - main
      - 'release/**'
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # JOB 1 — Hard block: PR targeting wrong branch.
  # Kept as its OWN job, unmerged with the informational checks below —
  # "🔴 Branch Target Check" is a REQUIRED status check on develop, main,
  # and release/** branch protection (confirmed live via the Branch
  # Protection API, 2026-08-25). Folding it into a combined job would
  # rename what GitHub sees as reporting that check, silently breaking
  # required-status-check enforcement (merges would block forever until
  # someone updated the branch protection settings to the new name) —
  # not worth the minutes saving. The other three checks below are not
  # required by any branch protection rule (confirmed the same way),
  # so those are safe to combine into one job.
  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  branch-target-guard:
    name: '🔴 Branch Target Check'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Block direct PRs to main from feature branches
        # github.base_ref/head_ref are attacker-controllable (a branch name
        # can contain shell metacharacters, e.g. $(...) command substitution)
        # and actionlint flags direct interpolation into an inline script as
        # a script-injection vector -- delivered via env: instead, same
        # pattern already used throughout qa.yml/deploy-preview.yml
        # (CodeRabbit flagged this correctly, 2026-08-26).
        env:
          BASE: ${{ github.base_ref }}
          HEAD: ${{ github.head_ref }}
        run: |
          echo "Base branch: $BASE"
          echo "Head branch: $HEAD"

          # Feature branches must not go directly to main
          if [[ "$BASE" == "main" && "$HEAD" == feature/* ]]; then
            echo ""
            echo "━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━"
            echo "🔴 INVALID BRANCH TARGET"
            echo "━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━"
            echo ""
            echo "Feature branches must target 'develop', not 'main'."
            echo ""
            echo "Correct flow: feature/* → develop → (release/*) → main"
            echo ""
            echo "Please update the base branch of this PR to 'develop'."
            echo "━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━"
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "✅ Branch target is valid."

  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # JOB 2 — Informational checks, combined (2026-08-25): Tier 1 warning,
  # Tier 2 warning, and cross-squad boundary detection used to be three
  # separate jobs, each paying GitHub Actions' 1-minute-per-job billing
  # floor even though each did only a few seconds of real work — roughly
  # 700 minutes/month of pure rounding overhead across this repo's PR
  # volume (see the 2026-08-25 Actions-minutes analysis). None of the
  # three is a required status check (confirmed live via the Branch
  # Protection API), so merging them changes nothing GitHub enforces —
  # only "🔴 Branch Target Check" above had to stay separate. Order
  # matters here: each check still runs and reports (posts its own
  # comment / log warning) regardless of whether an earlier one found
  # something, matching the old all-jobs-run-independently behavior —
  # nothing here calls exit 1, so a finding in one check never skips
  # the next.
  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  file-tier-checks:
    name: '🟡 File Tier & Squad Boundary Checks'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

      - name: Get changed Tier 1 files
        id: tier1
        uses: tj-actions/changed-files@2d756ea4c53f7f6b397767d8723b3a10a9f35bf2 # v44
        with:
          base_sha: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
          sha: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          files_yaml: |
            tier1:
              # Design tokens — owner: UI Designer
              - 'overrides/app/theme/foundation/**'
              - 'overrides/app/theme/index.ts'
              # Commerce SDK hooks (overrides surface) — owner: Integration Lead
              - 'overrides/app/hooks/use-current-basket.*'
              - 'overrides/app/hooks/use-current-customer.*'
              - 'overrides/app/hooks/use-einstein.*'
              - 'overrides/app/hooks/use-datacloud.*'
              - 'overrides/app/hooks/use-refresh-token.*'
              - 'overrides/app/hooks/use-multi-site.*'
              - 'overrides/app/hooks/use-navigation.*'
              # Runtime & integration config — owner: Integration Lead
              - 'config/**'
              - 'overrides/app/ssr.*'
              - 'worker/main.*'
              - 'mobify.config.js'
              - 'package.json'
              - 'package-lock.json'
              # Test & tooling config — owner: Integration Lead
              - 'vitest.config.*'
              - 'playwright.config.*'
              - '.storybook/**'
              - 'tests/lighthouserc.*'
              - 'lighthouserc.*'
              # CI/CD — owner: Integration Lead
              - '.github/workflows/**'
              # Governance — owner: Both Squad Leads + Integration Lead
              - 'AGENTS.md'
              - 'CLAUDE.md'
              - 'CODEOWNERS'
              - '.claude/rules/**'
              - '.claude/settings.json'
              - 'coderabbit.yaml'
              - '.coderabbit/**'
              - 'semgrep.yml'
              - 'scripts/hooks/**'

      - name: Warn if Tier 1 files changed (informational — not a merge block)
        if: steps.tier1.outputs.tier1_any_changed == 'true'
        run: |
          echo ""
          echo "━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━"
          echo "🔴 TIER 1 PROTECTED FILES DETECTED IN THIS PR"
          echo "━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━"
          echo ""
          echo "The following frozen files have been modified:"
          echo ""

content.text: One more thing worth chasing before I fan out reviewers: `ssr.js` sets `defaultCacheTimeSeconds: 600` for SSR'd pages. A nonce is only a meaningful security primitive if it's actually per-request — if the *entire* rendered response (headers + HTML body) gets cached and replayed for up to 10 minutes, the nonce becomes a value shared by every visitor who hits that cache entry during that window, not a true per-request secret. That's a real, non-obvious interaction the PR never mentions. Let me check how PWA Kit's SSR caching actually behaves before deciding whether this is worth raising.

content.content:
1	// helmet uses `export = helmet` (CommonJS), so ContentSecurityPolicyOptions must be
2	// imported from its submodule directly rather than from the package root.
3	import type { ContentSecurityPolicyOptions } from 'helmet/dist/middlewares/content-security-policy';
4	import type { IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from 'http';
5	import { randomBytes } from 'crypto';
6	
7	// SFCC-856 — nonce-based `style-src` so Chakra UI's runtime (emotion) style
8	// injection no longer needs a blanket 'unsafe-inline'. helmet 4.6.0's CSP
9	// directive values accept a function of (req, res) => string, invoked once
10	// per request (helmet/dist/middlewares/content-security-policy/index.d.ts),
11	// which is what makes a per-request nonce possible from this file alone —
12	// no change to ssr.js is required, since `contentSecurityPolicy` is already
13	// passed through to `helmet()` there as a plain value and is re-evaluated
14	// per request regardless.
15	//
16	// `res` is always the real Express Response at runtime — this config is
17	// only ever consumed by `helmet()` inside the Express app in ssr.js — but
18	// helmet's own directive-function type only declares the plain Node
19	// `http.ServerResponse` shape (no `.locals`). Widening the function's own
20	// parameter type to include `.locals` would make it a narrower (subtype)
21	// parameter than helmet's declared function type expects, which fails
22	// assignability under `strictFunctionTypes` (tsconfig.json has `strict:
23	// true`) — so the parameter stays typed exactly as the interface declares,
24	// and `.locals` access goes through a single, explained assertion instead.
25	type ResponseWithLocals = ServerResponse & { locals: Record<string, unknown> };
26	
27	const CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY = 'cspNonce';
28	
29	/**
30	 * Returns this request's CSP nonce, generating and caching it on
31	 * `res.locals` the first time it's requested so every directive that needs
32	 * it shares one value for the lifetime of the request. `res.locals` is the
33	 * same object `@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk`'s SSR render pipeline passes
34	 * straight through as the `locals` prop to `AppConfig`
35	 * (`overrides/app/components/_app-config/index.tsx`), which reads this same
36	 * key back off it to configure Chakra/emotion's style-tag cache with a
37	 * matching nonce — again with no ssr.js involvement, since that pass-through
38	 * already happens inside the SDK's own render pipeline.
39	 */
40	const getOrCreateNonce = (res: ServerResponse): string => {
41	  const resWithLocals = res as ResponseWithLocals; // see ResponseWithLocals comment above
42	  const existing = resWithLocals.locals[CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY];
43	  if (typeof existing === 'string') return existing;
44	  const nonce = randomBytes(16).toString('base64');
45	  resWithLocals.locals[CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY] = nonce;
46	  return nonce;
47	};
48	
49	export const contentSecurityPolicy: ContentSecurityPolicyOptions = {
50	  useDefaults: true,
51	  directives: {
52	    'img-src': [
53	      // Default source for product images - replace with your CDN
54	      '*.commercecloud.salesforce.com',
55	      '*.demandware.net',
56	      '*.adyen.com', // Payment gateways
57	      'pay.google.com', // Google Pay payment handler icon
58	      'www.gstatic.com', // optional, if icon is on gstatic
59	      // Contentful images
60	      'images.ctfassets.net',
61	    ],
62	    'script-src': [
63	      // Used by the service worker in /worker/main.js
64	      'storage.googleapis.com',
65	      // Connect to Google Cloud APIs
66	      'maps.googleapis.com',
67	      'places.googleapis.com',
68	      // Payment gateways
69	      '*.stripe.com',
70	      '*.paypal.com',
71	      '*.adyen.com',
72	      'pay.google.com',
73	      'www.gstatic.com',
74	      '*.demandware.net', // Used to load a valid payment scripts in test environment
75	      // Measmerize sizing widget (PDP)
76	      'client.measmerize.com',
77	      'static.client.measmerize.com',
78	    ],
79	    // SFCC-856 follow-up — split into `style-src-elem`/`style-src-attr` rather than one
80	    // combined `style-src`. CSP nonces can only ever apply to <style> ELEMENTS, never to a
81	    // raw inline `style="..."` ATTRIBUTE (there's no way to carry a nonce on an attribute
82	    // value) — but per the CSP3 spec, a nonce present anywhere in `style-src` disables
83	    // `'unsafe-inline'` for *everything* that directive governs, attributes included. A
84	    // combined `style-src` with both a nonce and 'unsafe-inline' therefore silently broke
85	    // every inline `style=` attribute in the app (e.g. the icon sprite sheet's
86	    // `style="position:absolute;width:0;height:0"` hiding technique) — confirmed live on the
87	    // MRT preview for this branch: a visible sprite sheet pushed a white gap above the page.
88	    // `style-src-elem` (the actual <style>/emotion-managed source: Chakra's runtime styling
89	    // plus the ZimmFontFace/ZimmTokensGlobal <Global> elements _app-config renders, all
90	    // sharing the nonce via the @emotion/react CacheProvider) keeps the nonce; `style-src-attr`
91	    // stays a plain 'unsafe-inline' with no nonce, since attributes have no nonce mechanism to
92	    // downgrade in the first place.
93	    //
94	    // `style-src` itself (CodeRabbit-flagged, correctly) still needs an explicit value even
95	    // though `style-src-elem`/`style-src-attr` cover every browser this app actually targets:
96	    // with `useDefaults: true` and no explicit `style-src` here, helmet 4.6.0 silently injects
97	    // its own default ('self' https: 'unsafe-inline') as the fallback for any browser that
98	    // doesn't understand the split directives, rather than us choosing that value on purpose.
99	    // Set explicitly below to the same conservative list this app used before nonces existed,
100	    // so the legacy-browser fallback is a deliberate, documented choice, not implicit helmet
101	    // behaviour.
102	    'style-src': ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'", 'static.client.measmerize.com'],
103	    'style-src-elem': [
104	      "'self'",
105	      (_req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse) => `'nonce-${getOrCreateNonce(res)}'`,
106	      "'unsafe-inline'", // CSP3 fallback for browsers predating nonce support

108	      // every color-mode change, including initial hydration) creates a raw <style> element

115	      // give a third-party DOM-API call our nonce. Fragile to a Chakra version bump: if this
116	      // exact string ever changes, recompute via
117	      // `node -e "console.log('sha256-' + require('crypto').createHash('sha256').update('<paste the new preventTransition() CSS string>','utf8').digest('base64'))"`.
118	      "'sha256-GNF74DLkXb0fH3ILHgILFjk1ozCF3SNXQ5mQb7WLu/Y='",

content.text: This is a significant finding: the Jira ticket title is **"CSP hardening: nonce/hash-based script-src and style-src (csp-xss)"** — but the PR only addresses `style-src`, declaring `script-src`'s issues "out of scope" in its own PR description, with no visible ticket comment confirming that narrowing. Let me check the ticket's comment thread for that, verify the "MRT platform injects unsafe-eval" claim, and check the live preview.

<result>## PR #79 Review Findings — Code Conventions & Structure

Reviewed against the live diff (`gh pr diff 79`) and the actual PR head commit (`8a6162750e`, branch `fix/SFCC-856-csp-hardening-v2`). Line numbers below are from that head commit. I independently verified the diff's own factual claims against the actual installed packages and SDK source rather than taking the comments at face value — details noted where relevant.

---

**1. Comment density — real judgment, not reflexive**

Roughly 84 of the 132 added lines (~64%) are comment-only. That's a genuinely high ratio, but I checked whether the density is padding or substance by independently verifying nearly every non-obvious factual claim made in these comments:

- helmet 4.6.0's `(req, res) => string` CSP directive-function signature (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:7-14`) — confirmed against `node_modules/helmet/dist/middlewares/content-security-policy/index.d.ts` and the installed version (4.6.0). Accurate.
- The `strictFunctionTypes` assignability reasoning (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:16-24`) — confirmed `tsconfig.json` has `strict: true`, and worked through the variance rule by hand: a call signature (not method-shorthand) is checked contravariantly, so narrowing `res`'s parameter type to `ResponseWithLocals` would indeed break assignability to helmet's declared type. Sound.
- `res.locals` being the same object passed as `AppConfig`'s `locals` prop — confirmed in `node_modules/@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk/ssr/server/react-rendering.js:317-318` (`React.createElement(AppConfig, {locals: res.locals})`). Accurate.
- The client's fresh/empty `locals` object — confirmed in `node_modules/@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk/ssr/browser/main.js:101-107` verbatim. Accurate (the comment cites the file as `main.jsx`; the real file is `main.js` — trivial, doesn't affect anything, mentioning only for completeness).
- The `sha256-GNF74DLkXb0fH3ILHgILFjk1ozCF3SNXQ5mQb7WLu/Y=` hash (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:118`) — recomputed independently from the actual `preventTransition()` string in `node_modules/@chakra-ui/color-mode/dist/color-mode.utils.js`. Byte-for-byte match.
- `react-helmet`'s ambient declaration already existing — confirmed in `overrides/app/types/vendor.d.ts:138-153`.

Given the subject matter (CSP is unforgiving — a wrong value fails silently until a browser blocks something in production) and that this is verifiably accurate, hard-won information (the sprite-sheet and `preventTransition()` bugs were apparently found live on MRT preview, per the PR body), I don't think this is over-documentation in the "explaining the obvious" sense conventions.md would object to. It's dense because the underlying interaction (CSP3 spec nuance + a third-party package's non-React DOM write + a TypeScript variance rule) is dense, not because the author padded it.

That said, two spots are genuinely disproportionate and could be trimmed without losing anything:
- `_app-config/index.tsx:102-107` — the `cspNonce?: string` field gets a 5-line comment; every sibling field in the same `AppLocals` type (`appConfig`, `site`, `locale`, `buildUrl`, `originalUrl`) has zero inline comment. A 1-2 line version pointing to the fuller explanation already given at `CSP_NONCE_META_NAME`'s declaration (lines 53-59) would match the surrounding file convention better.
- `contentSecurityPolicy.ts:29-39` — `getOrCreateNonce`'s JSDoc re-explains the same `res.locals` → `AppConfig` prop pass-through story already told in the comment block immediately above it (lines 7-24), two declarations earlier in the same file. This is direct, adjacent redundancy, not just "a lot of comments" — a tighter JSDoc describing the function's own contract (idempotent, caches on first call, returns a base64 nonce) with a pointer to the block above for the cross-file architecture would remove the duplication.

No rule in `conventions.md` sets an explicit comment-density ceiling (I checked — the closest stated rule is the commented-out-code rule, which is a different concern), so this is a judgment call, but a well-evidenced one: mostly justified, with two concrete, fixable instances of redundancy rather than a blanket problem.

**2. Naming**

`CSP_NONCE_META_NAME`, `CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY`, `getOrCreateNonce`, `ResponseWithLocals`, `emotionCache` are all correctly cased (SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants, PascalCase types, camelCase functions/variables) and consistent with established precedent in the same directory — `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` already uses `CLAIM`/`DELIMITER` SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants for the exact same magic-string-extraction purpose, and `_app-config/index.tsx` already imports SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants like `STORE_LOCATOR_RADIUS`/`DEFAULT_DNT_STATE`. No violation, high confidence.

One thing worth a second look, low-to-moderate confidence, no clean rule citation: the sha256 hash at `contentSecurityPolicy.ts:118` is a raw string literal inline in the `style-src-elem` array, not hoisted to a named constant the way `CSP_NONCE_META_NAME`/`CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY` were — despite having a whole paragraph next to it explaining it's fragile and needs manual recomputation on a Chakra bump. conventions.md's magic-string rule would seem to favor a named constant here (e.g. `CHAKRA_PREVENT_TRANSITION_STYLE_HASH`). Counter-argument: every other CSP directive value in this same file (`'self'`, `'unsafe-inline'`, `'*.stripe.com'`, etc.) is also a bare inline literal — the file's own established pattern treats directive arrays as literal-value lists, not constant references — so the hash is arguably consistent with that existing local convention rather than a deviation. I'd call this genuinely arguable rather than a clear violation.

Separately: `CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY = 'cspNonce'` (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:27`, written via bracket access) and `AppLocals.cspNonce` (`_app-config/index.tsx:107`, read via dot access) both spell `cspNonce`, but nothing mechanically links them — one is a runtime string constant, the other is a hardcoded property name in a type in a completely different file. Renaming `CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY`'s value alone wouldn't produce a compile error; it would just silently make `locals.cspNonce` always `undefined`, which would only surface as a live CSP violation in a browser, not in `tsc`/tests. Low confidence this is worth fixing (both files cross-reference each other by name in comments, so the practical drift risk is low), but it's a real, if narrow, gap — no shared source of truth for the key name across the two files.

**3. TypeScript idioms**

- `type ResponseWithLocals = ServerResponse & { locals: Record<string, unknown> }` (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:25`) and the cast `res as ResponseWithLocals` (line 41) — this is the correct escape hatch per typescript.md, and the inline comment pointing back to the fuller explanation is sound, not just present. I verified the underlying reasoning myself (see point 1) rather than taking the comment on faith, and it holds up: the parameter must stay typed as the plain `ServerResponse` helmet declares, so the cast has to happen inside the function body. Good design choice, too — the cast is encapsulated once inside `getOrCreateNonce` rather than pushed onto every call site.
- `Record<string, unknown>` for `.locals`, then narrowing via `typeof existing === 'string'` — this is a textbook-correct application of typescript.md's own guidance ("Prefer `unknown` with a type guard when the shape is genuinely not known at that point"). I don't think `AppLocals` should be reused here even though it exists: `AppLocals` describes the fully-populated shape as seen by the React `AppConfig` component *after* `AppConfig.restore()` runs; `contentSecurityPolicy.ts` operates earlier, at the Express/helmet middleware layer, before that population happens, and only ever touches one key. Importing a Tier 2 component file's local type into a Tier 1 SSR config file would also be a backwards dependency direction. Reasonable as-is, high confidence.
- `type` (not `interface`) for `ResponseWithLocals` — correct per typescript.md's default preference, and consistent with why the sibling `overrides/app/ssr/types.ts` deviates to `interface` for `SsrRes` (explicitly commented there: "`this` return type requires interface... for polymorphic self-type") — that reason doesn't apply here, so `type` is the right call.
- `readonly` — not applicable anywhere in this diff; `.locals` is deliberately mutated (nonce caching), so `readonly` would be wrong there, and correctly wasn't used.
- `import type { IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from 'http'` — correctly type-only; `randomBytes`, `CacheProvider`, `createCache`, `Helmet` are all correctly plain (value) imports since they're used at runtime. No misapplication either direction.

**4. Does `getOrCreateNonce`/`ResponseWithLocals` belong in this file?**

The function itself: yes, and I think this is closer to "the only viable place" than "reasonable minimal addition." `overrides/app/ssr.js` is absolutely frozen under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4 (no exception, unlike other Tier 1 files), and helmet's directive-value-as-function mechanism means the nonce logic can only live inside the config object `ssr.js` imports — i.e., this file. Not scope creep; it's the CSP policy's own implementation detail.

The type: more genuinely a judgment call. `overrides/app/ssr/types.ts` exists specifically for "minimal structural types for SSR Express handlers" to avoid a hard `@types/express` dependency, and every other sibling file that needs Express-adjacent types (`slasTokens.ts`, `marketingCloud.ts`, `paymentMetadata.ts` — 3 of 4 siblings) imports `SsrReq`/`SsrRes` from there rather than declaring locally. `ResponseWithLocals` is conceptually the same category of thing and currently duplicates that file's reason for existing, one level over. On the other hand: it has exactly one consumer today (conventions.md's DRY guidance says extract "once the same pattern appears in two places," not preemptively), and it's built differently from `types.ts`'s existing types — it intersects with the real Node `http.ServerResponse` rather than being a fully independent structural interface, because it has to satisfy helmet's exact declared function type under `strictFunctionTypes`. Moving it would mean introducing an `http` import into a file that currently has none and mixing two different typing strategies there. I'd call this a legitimate "worth a second look" rather than a rule violation in either direction.

**5. `AppLocals.cspNonce?: string` placement/documentation**

Placement (`_app-config/index.tsx:107`, appended after `originalUrl?`) matches convention — all fields are optional with bare `?`, new field added at the end, same style. Comment length does not match convention — see point 1's first bullet; every sibling field in this type has zero comment, `cspNonce` gets five lines. The imbalance is explainable (this is the one field whose value doesn't originate from `AppConfig.restore()` in this same file, unlike its siblings), but proportionally it stands out, and could be trimmed.

**6. console.log / debug statements / commented-out code**

None found. I grepped every added line (`+` in the diff) for `console.`, `debugger`, `TODO`, `FIXME`, `XXX` — the only match is inside a comment documenting a maintenance command (`` `node -e "console.log(...)"` `` at `contentSecurityPolicy.ts:117`, a recipe for recomputing the hash if Chakra changes), not an actual runtime `console.log` call. I also re-read every added comment block manually; all are prose explanations, none are disabled/commented-out code. Clean.

**7. Other findings**

- `@emotion/cache` (`_app-config/index.tsx:10`) is imported for the first time anywhere in this codebase, and — like `@emotion/react` and `react-helmet`, both already used elsewhere (`overrides/app/theme/fontFace.tsx`, `overrides/app/theme/zimmTokensGlobal.tsx`, `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/index.tsx`) — it's not declared in root `package.json` at all; it resolves only because it's a transitive dependency of the already-used `@emotion/react`. This isn't a new pattern this PR introduces (the same "undeclared transitive dependency" situation already exists for `@emotion/react` itself in Tier 1 theme files), and no `package.json`/lockfile edit occurred, so I don't think Hard Rule #7 is actually implicated — flagging only because it's the kind of thing that could break silently on an unrelated dependency-tree reshuffle. Low confidence this needs action; mentioning for completeness only.
- On the separately-tracked missing-test question: I agree it's a defensible should-fix, not a must-fix, under testing.md's own bar. `getOrCreateNonce`'s caching branch (return existing vs. generate-and-store) is exactly "pure logic that would survive a refactor invisibly if broken" — a regression there (e.g., losing the cache-and-reuse behavior, or generating a nonce that doesn't match between the header and the meta tag) wouldn't be caught by `tsc`, lint, or any existing test, only by a live CSP violation. That said, testing it requires mocking a `ServerResponse`-shaped object, which is minor friction, not a blocker. I'd weigh it the same way the tracked item does: worth adding, not worth blocking on.

**Not flagged, considered and ruled out:** repeated literal directive values (`'self'`, `'unsafe-inline'`, `'static.client.measmerize.com'`) across `style-src`/`style-src-elem`/`style-src-attr` — this matches the file's own pre-existing, unchanged convention of repeating origin strings across directives (`'*.stripe.com'` etc. already repeat across `script-src`/`connect-src`/`frame-src`), so holding the new code to a stricter DRY standard than the rest of the file wasn't consistent. Also ruled out: forward-referencing `isServerSide` (declared at line 266) from inside `cspNonce`'s resolution at line 161 — safe, since `AppConfig` the function isn't invoked until after full module evaluation completes; not a TDZ bug.</result>

<result>Investigation complete. I read both changed files at the PR head, the diff, `ssr.js`, and then went deep into `node_modules` (helmet, express, `@emotion/react`/`cache`, `@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk`, `@salesforce/pwa-kit-runtime`, and the actual installed `lighthouse`/`csp_evaluator` packages) plus live-tested the PR's own MRT preview with repeated `curl` requests. Two of the findings below are substantive and not covered by the pre-verified list; the rest are smaller confirmations from the five specific angles requested.

## Findings

**1. CDN caching defeats the nonce's per-request uniqueness on the site's two highest-traffic page types — HIGH confidence, empirically verified live.**
`overrides/app/pages/home/index.tsx:117-118` and `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/index.tsx:180` both call `res.set('Cache-Control', 's-maxage=..., stale-while-revalidate=...')` (pre-existing, not touched by this PR). I curled the PR's live preview 5 times in a row:
```
x-cache: Hit from cloudfront   (all 5 requests)
cache-control: s-maxage=900, stale-while-revalidate=900
age: 60, 62, 63, 64, 65        (climbing — same cached object)
style-src-elem ... 'nonce-Qh5r+26oiEGz+ogUaJVySQ==' ...   (identical on all 5 hits)
```
`getOrCreateNonce` in `overrides/app/ssr/contentSecurityPolicy.ts:38-46` does generate a fresh, cryptographically random nonce per *origin* request — that part is correct. But once CloudFront caches that response for 900s (confirmed live), the exact same nonce is replayed to every visitor of that cached page for the full cache lifetime. A nonce's entire security value rests on being unpredictable *before* the response exists; here, anyone (including an attacker) can read the current nonce off any normal page load and reuse it for the whole cache window. This doesn't break rendering or produce console errors — it silently downgrades the nonce, for homepage/PDP specifically, to roughly the strength of a static allowlist for up to 15 minutes at a time. Neither the PR nor the ticket mentions this interaction. It isn't fixable inside the two changed files — the standard fix (edge-compute nonce rewrite on cache HIT, e.g. a CloudFront Function) lives outside `overrides/` entirely, and the alternative (stop caching HTML) conflicts with this project's stated mobile-perf priority. Worth a conscious team decision, not a blocker on its own — it's still strictly better than the pre-PR always-open `'unsafe-inline'` for anything uncached.

**2. Lighthouse's `csp-xss` audit never evaluates `style-src` at all — this PR cannot move the metric the ticket names, verified against this repo's own installed packages.**
Traced `node_modules/lighthouse/lighthouse-core/audits/csp-xss.js` → `node_modules/csp_evaluator/lighthouse/lighthouse_checks.ts`'s `evaluateForFailure()` (the sole function whose output determines the audit's score: `score = bypasses.length ? 0 : 1`). It runs exactly: `checkMissingScriptSrcDirective`, `checkMissingObjectSrcDirective`, `checkMultipleMissingBaseUriDirective`, `checkStrictDynamic`, `checkScriptUnsafeInline`, `checkWildcards`, `checkPlainUrlSchemes`. Every one of these is hardcoded to `script-src`/`object-src`/`base-uri` — the last two via `DIRECTIVES_CAUSING_XSS = [SCRIPT_SRC, OBJECT_SRC, BASE_URI]` in `csp_evaluator/checks/security_checks.ts:33-34`. `style-src`/`style-src-elem`/`style-src-attr` appear in none of these checks and nowhere in the finding-to-message map either. Applying this to the actual live header I captured, the specific, current trigger is very likely `checkStrictDynamic`: this app's `script-src` is a plain host allowlist (`storage.googleapis.com`, `*.stripe.com`, etc.) with no `'strict-dynamic'`, which that checker treats as a score-zeroing finding — not `'unsafe-eval'` (there's no dedicated unsafe-eval check in this audit) and not style-src. Practical upshot: the Jira ticket's premise that style-src's `'unsafe-inline'` contributes to the failing `csp-xss` audit appears to be factually wrong for this specific Lighthouse check, so this PR — however well-built — will not close that finding; only the script-src work the PR declares out of scope can. (Separately confirmed: this repo's own `lighthouserc.js` uses the `lighthouse:recommended` preset, which per `node_modules/@lhci/utils/src/presets/recommended.js` doesn't assert on `csp-xss` individually anyway, so this isn't currently a CI-blocking gate either way — it's presumably tracked from a manual/external Lighthouse run.) The style-src work remains a legitimate, independent hardening improvement on its own merits; it just isn't the fix for the audit named in the ticket.

**3. `defaultPwaKitSecurityHeaders` forcibly re-merges `'unsafe-eval'` + wildcard hosts into `script-src` on every response — confirms the PR's "not fixable from this repo" framing, with a sharper mechanism than the PR itself states.**
`overrides/app/ssr.js` runs `app.use(defaultPwaKitSecurityHeaders)` before `app.use(helmet({contentSecurityPolicy}))`. That function (`node_modules/@salesforce/pwa-kit-runtime/utils/middleware/security.js:25-77`) monkey-patches `res.setHeader` so that *any* later call setting the CSP header — including helmet's own — gets union-merged with a required set containing `'script-src': ["'self'", "'unsafe-eval'", runtimeAdmin, '*.site.com']`. So even if `contentSecurityPolicy.ts`'s own script-src array never mentioned `'unsafe-eval'`, the final response would still carry it; the only way to stop that is to stop calling this middleware in `ssr.js`, which is absolutely frozen (Hard Rule 4, no exception). Bonus finding: this repo's own script-src array doesn't include `'self'` at all — the app's own bundle scripts structurally depend on this merge just to load. Confirmed this merge's required-directive set has no `style-src*` entries, so it has zero interaction with this PR's actual changes. Forward-looking note for whoever scopes script-src next: a future nonce/`strict-dynamic` script-src would get the same forced re-merge, undermining much of its value unless addressed — not a defect in this PR, just context worth having going in.

**4–10, confirmatory checks (no defect found; reported since they were explicitly asked about):**
- **TypeScript soundness of `ResponseWithLocals` cast** (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:41`): sound. `node_modules/express/lib/middleware/init.js:38` (`res.locals = res.locals || Object.create(null)`) guarantees `res.locals` is a real object on every request before any user middleware runs.
- **Memoization / per-request cache** (`_app-config/index.tsx:164`): correct, and better than a hypothetical shared default cache — creating a fresh `createCache()` per request (since `cspNonce` differs per request) is Emotion's own documented SSR pattern and avoids the classic "shared cache mutated across requests" SSR footgun.
- **Ordering/race check**: `node_modules/helmet/dist/middlewares/content-security-policy/index.js` evaluates directive functions and calls `res.setHeader` synchronously inside its own `app.use` middleware, which runs before `app.get('*', runtime.render)` later in the chain — so `res.locals.cspNonce` is always populated before `AppConfig` renders. No race.
- **Storybook divergence** (`.storybook/preview.tsx`): mounts `ChakraProvider` with no `CacheProvider`/nonce. Confirmed immaterial — Storybook doesn't enforce the app's CSP header. Confirmed no other file in `overrides/` imports `_app-config` directly (all other grep hits are comments referencing it by name), so nothing else assumes the old tree shape.
- **`style-src-attr: 'unsafe-inline'` carve-out**: confirmed narrow and currently risk-free in this codebase specifically — `overrides/app/utils/richText.tsx` (the only rich-text/CMS renderer touching `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`-adjacent territory) explicitly discards every HTML attribute when converting SFCC copy to React elements, so CMS content can never produce a live inline `style=` attribute. The only real `style={{...}}` usages in the codebase are static developer literals (`zimmLogo`, and an unrelated scaffold page).
- **`@emotion/cache` phantom dependency**: not declared in `package.json` (neither is `@emotion/react`, which is already imported the same way pre-existing this PR in `theme/zimmTokensGlobal.tsx`/`theme/fontFace.tsx`). Low risk — `@emotion/cache` is a hard dependency of `@emotion/react` per `package-lock.json`, so it's guaranteed present wherever `@emotion/react` already resolves; this PR just extends an already-accepted pattern.
- **No `res.locals.cspNonce` collision**: grepped `overrides/app/ssr/{paymentMetadata,marketingCloud,slasTokens}.ts` on the PR branch — none read or write that key.

No other correctness, hydration, or regression risks turned up beyond the above and what was already given as pre-verified.</result>

content.text: That correctness agent surfaced two very consequential findings — one converges with and sharpens something I'd already flagged (nonce defeated by CDN caching, now with live empirical proof), and one is a potential bombshell: that Lighthouse's `csp-xss` audit doesn't evaluate `style-src` at all, meaning this PR might not actually close the finding it's named for. Given how much that second claim could reshape the scope verdict, I need to verify both myself against primary sources before presenting either as fact.
